title: North-South Inequality
subtitle: A two-speed world
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The richest 10% of the planet take more than half of all world income. And yet extreme poverty is a quarter of what it was thirty years ago.

hero.hook: An American earns in one hour what someone in Niger earns in a full day of work.

blocks.text: The gap between rich and poor countries remains one of the most striking facts about the world today. Globalization promised that living standards would draw closer, but the differences in wealth between nations are still enormous.

Recent history is not all dark, though. Extreme poverty has retreated faster over the past thirty years than ever before. This course looks at the roots of these inequalities, and at the reasons for that strange paradox.
The **richest 10%** of the world's population take more than 52% of global income. The poorest 50% share just 8% of the pie. Wealth has never been this concentrated in human history.

The divide shows up in life expectancy too: 83 years in Japan, but 55 years in the Central African Republic. These gaps are not accidents. They come from deeply unequal access to clean water, food and health care.
In one hour of work, the average resident of the United States earns as much as someone in Niger earns in a whole day.

sections.title: Historical roots that are still alive

blocks.text: To understand these gaps you have to go back to colonization. The European powers organized many territories of the South as suppliers of raw materials (coffee, cocoa, cotton), and held back their industrialization to protect their own factories.

blocks.caption: The wealth gap between North and South remains among the widest on the planet

blocks.text: The same logic continues today through the [[terms of trade]]: countries in the South mostly sell raw materials whose prices swing wildly, while they buy manufactured goods whose prices only go up. Debt adds to the weight, since paying the interest sometimes takes a bigger share of a national budget than education or health.

The past thirty years have still brought a spectacular retreat of absolute poverty, which affected 36% of the world's population in 1990 and less than 10% before 2020. That progress comes above all from the dazzling growth of China and India.

The progress has a hidden face, and that is what the [[“elephant curve”]] drawn by the economist Branko Milanovic shows. Incomes exploded for the Asian middle classes, while working-class incomes in rich countries stagnated under the pressure of global competition. Narrowing the gap between countries did not prevent new tensions inside the rich countries themselves.

The future of North-South inequality is now being decided on climate. The countries of the South, historically the least responsible for greenhouse gas emissions, are the most exposed to droughts, floods and rising seas.

To close these gaps for good, the international community is exploring new routes: [[official development assistance]] targeted at the energy transition, or canceling the debt of the most fragile countries. As long as the wealth of the richest grows faster than the wealth of the poorest, the tensions will stay high.

The richest 10% in the world take more than half of global income, but extreme poverty has fallen faster in thirty years than ever before, thanks to the rise of China and India. The next great challenge along this North-South divide will be climate.
